https://www.dw.com/en/could-pakistan-s-j.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5J4z0 Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 on corruption charges Image: Arif Ali/AFP Advertisement Pakistan's Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan to be shifted to a private hospital after Khan's family and political supporters repeatedly raised concerns about the 73-year-old's deteriorating health in Rawalpindi's Adiala jail. The founder of the opposition party Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has been imprisoned since August 2023 and is currently serving a 14-year sentence on corruption charges he says are politically motivated. The former prime minister was ousted in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Khan and his supporters say Pakistan's influential military is trying to keep him out of politics, an allegation the military has denied. Despite remaining behind bars, Khan remains politically popular. After a crackdown on the PTI following Khan's arrest, the candidates backed by him performed strongly in the February 2024 election. "Three years in prison have not removed Khan from Pakistani politics. He remains PTI's biggest political asset, but the party's reliance on him has also exposed weaknesses in its leadership and organization," Raza Rumi, a US-based Pakistani political analyst, told DW. Dousing speculation of new deal for Khan The transfer of Khan to the Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad for medical assessment has added a new dimension to the debate over his future and the possibility of political negotiations. However, Khan's adviser Sayed Zulfi Bukhari rejected speculation that the court decision was the result of any political deal with the government. "There is no deal between Imran Khan and anyone. This is the Supreme Court's decision, which is very much welcomed," Bukhari said. Pakistan's Law Minister Azam Nazeer Tarar said in a video statement on Tuesday night that the government would challenge the Supreme Court order , claiming it was unlawful. The minister said a convicted prisoner must be treated inside the jail or at a public hospital according to law, adding that he was requesting Khan's medical tests be carried out at a government hospital instead of a private facility. "Legally, Khan has not been granted bail nor have his convictions been suspended. He will remain a prisoner, and the hospital executive ward shall serve as a sub-jail. Unfortunately, most ordinary prisoners with far more serious ailments are never allowed such facilities by the courts," Osama Malik, a legal expert, told DW. Pakistan's Minister of State for Interior, Talal Chaudhry, told DW that "Khan's cases will be decided by the courts." Khan's health problems carry 'major political consequences' PTI's Bukhari told DW that Khan "hasn't been receiving the right medical care in prison." "That is why it has got to this stage. He has been kept in complete solitude, which has deteriorated his health," said Bukhari. The PTI party has said Khan is suffering from various health conditions , including poor eyesight, fluctuations in blood pressure and anxiety linked to restricted contact with his family, and has been unable to access specialist medical care. Can Pakistan still help end the US-Iran war? "Beyond the medical issues, this is also about trust. The PTI and Khan's family have repeatedly questioned his access to doctors and the transparency of his treatment," said analyst Rumi. "After three years in prison, and given his age, any deterioration in his health carries major political consequences. The state, therefore, has every reason to ensure credible and transparent medical care," he added. The court has also ordered a medical board, including Khan's sister, Dr. Uzma Khan, and personal physician Dr. Faisal Sultan, to oversee Khan's treatment. What future for Khan and his PTI party? Khan's continued imprisonment has tested the PTI's ability to maintain its political strength, and the party's future will depend on whether it can maintain support without the direct political presence of its figurehead. "Khan's political future does not look bright; he will have to compromise his political future. He will remain in jail, and even if his PTI party comes to power in the future, Khan will not be part of the government," Qamar Cheema, a political analyst, told DW. At the same time, Khan's continued popularity makes it difficult for authorities to remove him completely from the political equation in Pakistan . "For the state, the dilemma remains: keeping Khan imprisoned has not neutralized his influence, while releasing him without a broader settlement could revive the confrontation," said Rumi. Rumi added that any lasting political settlement with Khan would likely require an understanding with the military establishment, which remains a key stakeholder in Pakistan. "Such a deal could involve legal relief for Khan, greater political space for PTI, and eventually his release, in return for PTI easing its confrontation with the military and pursuing a negotiated political process. But deep mistrust remains a major obstacle, while Khan's reluctance to compromise limits the prospects for a settlement," he said. Analyst Cheema said he doesn't think there is any possibility of a deal between the government and Khan. "This was a genuine understanding in the Supreme Court that he should have been given proper health care," he said. Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A jailer in Nelson county, Kentucky, with an electric shock glove on 13 August 2026. Photograph: Dylan Lovan/AP View image in fullscreen A jailer in Nelson county, Kentucky, with an electric shock glove on 13 August 2026. Photograph: Dylan Lovan/AP Nebraska Nebraska school district asks police to stop using shock gloves on students Omaha police agreed to stop carrying electric shock gloves in the halls of state’s largest public school district Associated Press Sat 22 Aug 2026 10.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Omaha police recently agreed to stop carrying gloves that can deliver electric shocks to students in the halls of Nebraska ’s largest public school district. The decision affecting most Omaha middle and high schools came after the Associated Press first revealed Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE )’s plan to give officers the “Gloves” – or “generated low output voltage emitters”. The devices have also been used in recent years by some jails. The superintendent of Omaha public schools, Matthew Ray, on 18 August requested that police working in the schools, known as school resource officers, stop using the gloves. Omaha police agreed two days later. Their cities dropped Flock surveillance cameras. They’re still being watched Read more However, the suburban Bellevue police department that patrols two Omaha schools and the large Bellevue district said its officers will continue carrying the gloves. Three other large school districts in the metro area that have Omaha school resource officers assigned to their buildings have not taken action to stop police from using the devices. The AP left messages seeking comment from the Millard, Elkhorn and Westside districts that are also patrolled by Omaha officers. Bellevue schools spokesperson Amanda Oliver said the district has a great relationship with Bellevue police and doesn’t see a need to alter anything. “We’ve got a great communication and dialogue that we have with them consistently. And so for us right now, no changes are being made,” Oliver said. Ray said in a school board meeting on 17 August and in a letter to the public schools community that he’d only learned about the gloves the previous week. But local television station KETV found emails from 2023, when Omaha police notified the districts that the department planned to equip officers with the gloves, and an official with the Omaha district said they were already familiar with them because Bellevue police had them at two Omaha schools. Students in all the Omaha area districts have gone back to class over the past two weeks. Before halting the use of the gloves, the Omaha police department held a news conference in which an officer demonstrated how they can help an officer quickly get control of someone who is refusing commands. Omaha police used the gloves twice during the 2025-26 school year. And Bellevue police have also used them twice in previous years. At the school board meeting, about 30 people spoke out against police using the gloves. Residents and board members alike said they were appalled at the practice. No one spoke in favor of it. “I can’t even imagine walking down the hallway and seeing a peer of mine being electrocuted in a place that is supposed to be a safe space for students,” said Nora Wessel, a senior at Omaha Central high school. “Yet, this is now a very real possibility. These are adults we are supposed to be able to trust, but these weapons create a barrier for our students to turn to resource officers when needed.” Ken Trump, president of the consulting firm National School Safety and Security Services, said before schools allow police to bring in technology like shock gloves, there should be a careful discussion of questions like how school resource officers will respond to students with disabilities or special medical needs, how parents will be informed and under what circumstances the gloves can be used. “Less than lethal doesn’t mean low risk,” Trump said. Ray said the district recognized longstanding relationships with law enforcement partners and the important role school resource officers have in promoting school safety. Continued use of the gloves “would be counterproductive to our work together”, Ray said. Omaha’s mayor, John Ewing Jr, who helped oversee creating the school resource officer program when he was on the police force, said the department has honored the school district’s decision to “opt out”. The Omaha police department said officers will continue to carry stun guns, batons, pepper spray and firearms. Most of the Omaha police department’s 34 school resource officers had been trained and were allowed to use the gloves, the mayor and the police chief, Todd Schmaderer, said in a statement. “We believe it is the safest use-of-force option in the rare times when it is used,” the statement said. In 2025, Omaha police agreed to pay Compliant Technologies LLC, which manufactures the gloves, about $66,000 for 40 gloves, according to the contract. Officers were expected to give warning before using the gloves and then touch the person for up to 15 seconds while the electric shock was delivered, the statement said. Bellevue’s police chief, Ken Clary, said his officers will continue carrying the gloves, which they have had for more than three years. “I am not comfortable having our officers give up a tool that has repeatedly proven to be safe, effective and less harmful than the alternatives,” Clary said in a statement. The devices activate when an officer presses a button. The gloves must touch someone’s skin directly to produce voltage that causes pain, which is intended to make people stop resisting officers. Unlike stun guns, they do not leave burn or contact marks. In the 2025-26 school year, an Omaha officer used the glove in one case to stop a high school student from another school from trying to escape after fighting with a security guard, according to the statement. In a second case, the glove was used on a student at the Omaha district’s integrated learning center for special education students. Police said that student made verbal threats and threw a chair at a school security guard, striking the guard in the head. The student also punched the guard in the head, according to the statement. Bellevue police didn’t immediately have details about when its officers have used the gloves. Clary said the devices have been an extremely effective tool that sometimes make students cooperate on sight even without shocking a student. Omaha public schools is Nebraska’s largest school district and serves more than 50,000 students, its website says. The metro area’s other districts are also among the biggest in the state. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Cody Butler, the 21-year-old former chair of the One Nation Conservative Network at the Lib Dems conference in Brighton on Sunday. Photograph: Alexandra Topping/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Cody Butler, the 21-year-old former chair of the One Nation Conservative Network at the Lib Dems conference in Brighton on Sunday. Photograph: Alexandra Topping/The Guardian Liberal Democrat conference Feeling ‘forced out’ by Badenoch? Lib Dems conference welcomes young Tory defectors Self-described moderates say Ed Davey’s party offers them a home as Conservatives shift further right Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Sun 20 Sep 2026 14.04 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 15.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Climbing the party-branded stairs of the Brighton Centre with a Liberal Britain tote bag over his shoulder, Cody Butler looks quite at home at the Liberal Democrats’ annual jamboree. But asked how he is finding it, the 21-year-old replied: “Odd.” The former Tory activist resigned as chair of the One Nation Conservative Network and left his old party in July, arguing that centrists, remainers and members worried about the climate crisis and conservation were no longer welcome in the party. A week ago, he joined the Lib Dems . “There is no easy way to describe joining a new political party, because it’s like finding a new family,” he said. “I was brought up in a Conservative association. I was the local Tory boy. So it’s great, but odd.” Butler is one of several youthful former Tories who have publicly defected to Britain’s third party and are in the process of setting up a new group: the One Nation Liberals. It’s a growing group, with other potential defectors believed to be waiting to see if they can survive in Kemi Badenoch’s increasingly rightwing party. Butler has been joined by Josh Bancroft, a former Tory councillor on Cannock Chase council, who left the party to join the Lib Dems earlier this month. “Moderates like me have been forced out of the big tent over the past few years,” he said. “My politics haven’t changed, but the party has.” The 26-year-old said moderates looking for the exit have grown in number since Badenoch embarked on a purge of the Conservative parliamentary party . In July, the Tory leader warned that anyone who supported net zero targets or Britain’s membership of the European convention on human rights would be blocked from standing as a candidate in the next election. The former minister Gavin Barwell lost the whip , and another former cabinet member, Grant Shapps, was blocked from standing again for the party. View image in fullscreen Ed Davey taking part in a Q&A session with the journalist Carolyn Quinn at the Lib Dems conference on Sunday. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA “The Conservatives have taken leaps to the right and left me and millions of voters behind,” Bancroft added. “The Liberal Democrats can be and should be their new political home.” Bancroft and Butler have been welcomed with open arms into the Liberal ranks, with one MP joking that Badenoch had become the Lib Dems’ most effective recruiter. During a Q&A on the first full day of the conference, party leader Ed Davey repeatedly mentioned Badenoch, referencing her decision to freeze out members and MPs who support net zero policies. “Unlike Kemi Badenoch, who thinks there wasn’t a problem with this summer’s heatwaves, we actually realise you have to take action on climate change and we’re leading that debate,” he said. Despite being stuck at about 11% in national polling, many Liberal Democrat activists and MPs in Brighton are talking with atypical swagger about cementing the foundations of the so-called orange wall. They point to the 72 seats they won in the last election, making them the largest third party in British politics for over a century. And of the 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024 , 20 were taken by the Conservatives. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion When asked if reaching 100 seats by taking those targets was the aim, Davey insisted there was “no ceiling” to the Liberal Democrats’ ambitions. “If we have great local councillors, great local candidates and great local campaigners, we can beat Reform, the Tories, Labour, Green, the SNP, anyone. We can win anywhere where there’s a multiparty fight.” On Sunday, Davey explicitly ruled out any future pact with the Tories. But when asked about an arrangement with Labour, he said maximising the number of Lib Dem MPs would give his party a stronger hand in any future negotiations. “That means you have to box really smartly,” he said. While that prospect may have some pure-blood Tories running for the hills, it could lure others into the Liberal Democrat ranks, argued Butler. “It used to be that if you wanted power you could only join the Conservatives or Labour, but that reality doesn’t exist any more in a five-party system,” he said. “My message to other One Nation Conservatives is: you can be true to what you believe, and if you back the Liberal Democrats, you’re actually backing the future kingmakers of government. They will write the budget. The Conservatives won’t.” Explore more on these topics Liberal Democrat conference Liberal Democrats Conservatives Kemi Badenoch Ed Davey news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/30/isla.text: As transnational criminal networks deploy increasingly sophisticated technology to conceal illicit wealth, authorities across the globe are accelerating efforts to dismantle international financial crime. These priorities framed the agenda in Azerbaijan as delegates convened for the Third High-Level Meeting of the Heads of Anti-Corruption Law Enforcement Agencies of Member States of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). At the core of the summit was the implementation of the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention. According to the OIC, the landmark treaty represents the first multilateral anti-corruption law enforcement agreement tailored specifically for Islamic Cooperation member states, establishing a unified legal foundation to track illicit financial flows across borders. Overcoming bureaucratic borders Cross-border financial investigations often face significant legal barriers, a challenge highlighted alongside Malaysia’s recent asset recovery experience.Abd Halim Bin Aman, Chief Commissioner of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission, detailed his agency’s multi-year effort to trace and repatriate stolen funds following the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) case."We managed to achieve our goal of tackling the 1MDB matter and as of today we managed to bring back home about 75% to 80% to outside countries, and we managed to bring back about 33 billion Malaysian ringgit worth of loss," he revealed. Originally established in 2009 as a state-owned strategic development fund, 1MDB became well-known for being embroiled in one of the world's largest financial kleptocracy scandals, after billions of dollars were systematically siphoned off through offshore shell companies and international bank accounts.According to the US Justice Department’s website, between 2009 and 2015, money was "laundered through major financial institutions worldwide, including in the United States, Switzerland, Singapore, and Luxembourg" and "misappropriated more than $4.5 billion (approximately €4 billion) in funds belonging to 1MDB through a criminal scheme."The Justice Department stated it "repatriated an additional $156 million (approximately €139 million) in misappropriated 1MDB funds" to people from Malaysia and brought the total of returned funds to approximately $1.4 billion (approximately €1.2 billion). Bin Aman also shared his views on what typically slows down such international matters. "Bureaucracy is always being an obstacle to any investigation," he said. He said that the summit provides a necessary platform to share legislation and best practices to speed up investigations irrespective of legal backgrounds.Ivica Bošnjak, Deputy Minister of Security for Bosnia and Herzegovina, outlined the unique structural and geographical pressures facing his country."Bosnia and Herzegovina is complicated and complex in the political part, and therefore the organization of the entire security system is complex," Bošnjak stated.He noted that national authorities must coordinate "16 police agencies and a whole series of other law enforcement agencies" operating across the security sector.While the state has adopted extensive legal regulations and action plans, Bošnjak told Euronews that "much still needs to be done to refine a couple of more crucial laws" and operational strategies to tackle cross-border financial crime effectively.Building a global enforcement coalition Tugay Rahimli, Special Assistant to the Prosecutor General of Azerbaijan, outlined the scale and primary objective of the summit."Today's event brings together more than 250 participants from 46 member and service states as well as eight international organisations," Rahimli said."The main objective of today's event is to facilitate and foster international cooperation among member states, facilitate exchange of information and best practices, as well as to enhance the joint efforts to recover the assets obtained through crime," he added.Rahimli also pointed to a key leadership development for the host nation."Particularly important outcomes of today's event that I would like to highlight is the election of Azerbaijan to chair the bureau for the next two years," he told Euronews.A unified legal framework Kamran Aliyev, Prosecutor General of the Republic of Azerbaijan, confirmed the host nation's immediate legislative steps regarding the agreement, the Makkah al-Mukarramah Convention, which is an agreement designed to facilitate mutual legal assistance, the exchange of information, and the recovery of assets derived through corruption. "This convention first was adopted in 2022 in the city of Makkah, of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, and this is a new platform in fighting corruption at a regional level," Aliyev said. The agreement operates under a framework, which incorporates 57 nations, with the intention to bypass lengthy diplomatic channels and to allow law enforcement agencies to share intelligence quickly, conduct joint investigations, and trace, freeze, and return stolen state funds to their countries of origin. Aliyev said that Azerbaijan has joined international initiatives and international and regional conventions against corruption and has also "implemented all provisions of the conventions into our legislation."Fighting tech with tech Imed Hazgui, President of the High Authority for Administrative and Financial Control in Tunisia, talked about the global nature of the conference and how the meeting "brings together about fifty Islamic states who are interested in the development of cooperation between them in the fight against corruption."He warned about the methods modern criminals may use to evade international sanctions."Today we all know that terrorist groups and organised crime groups are increasingly using developed technologies to commit their crimes, to hide the necessary means of having them, and also to escape all sanctions," he said.He is urging member states to integrate advanced digital tools into their law enforcement strategies to keep pace with these threats, which he says "requires a great cooperation at the level of the exchange of developed technologies, of the exchanges of the good practices in this sense, through also the increasingly use of artificial intelligence today in the fight against corruption, in the prediction of dangers and in the treatment of dangers."
